title: Data Visualization Influencers: Tracing the Creation and Curation Strategies Behind Propagandist Visualizations on X
abstract: Data visualization is increasingly understood as a political process shaped by creators' editorial design and data choices. Prior research has examined how such choices produce deceptive visualizations, focusing on social media users' misleading visualizations of public data. This overlooks how creators draw on professional expertise to produce propagandist visualizations of political narratives. We investigate visualization creators who design and share propagandist visualizations of political claims, such as immigration, criminality, and others, in US online discourse. Extending prior work on data visualization as propaganda, we present an exploratory study of 17 creators and the propagandist visualizations they create and curate for political discourse on X. We introduce the notion of a ``data visualization influencer'': an online creator who (1) leverages perceived credibility as a data expert, and (2) engages in epistemic capture of the credibility aesthetics of data and visualizations to manufacture propaganda. We discuss implications for research and practice.
repository: arXiv (Cornell University)

title: Research on the Application of Data Visualization in Management Accounting Decision-Making
abstract: In the era of digital economy, enterprise financial management is faced with the dilemma of data overload and lack of information, and data visualization has become an important tool to connect data and management accounting decision-making. This paper studies the application areas and implementation effects of data visualization in management accounting decision-making, aiming to provide a reference for the digital transformation of enterprise finance. This study adopted the literature review method and conducted an inductive analysis based on the relevant theme literature included in CNKI. Through the literature review, it is found that data visualization can improve the readability and interactivity of financial information, and help management accounting not only to output information, but also to participate more in the business decision-making of enterprises. Sound data governance, suitable analysis tools and interdisciplinary professionals are an important basis for the application of visualization technology. This study also discusses the challenges in practice and provides suggestions for future research.
venue: Advances in Economics Management and Political Sciences

title: The Role of Python and SQL in Transforming Data Visualization for Enhanced Analytical Efficiency
authors: Subodh Kumar Yadav, Dr. Renu Bagoria, Mr. Suraj Yadav; Renu Bagoria; Suraj Yadav
abstract: These days, we’re dealing with more data than ever before. To make sense of it all, we need good data visualization. It’s not just nice to have – it’s a must-have for making smart decisions in any industry. This study systematically investigates how the integration of Python and SQL can streamline and optimize data visualization workflows, offering a reproducible and scalable analyt-ical framework. Through a systematic review of five key studies, we examine how Python’s visualization libraries (Matplotlib, Seaborn, Plotly) provide flexibility, customization, and interactivity, while SQL enables efficient data extraction, aggregation, and preparation. We˛cławski et al. (2026) compared commercial tools and Python li-braries, concluding that Python offers greater programmability for complex visualizations. Guo et al. (2024) demonstrated a real-world pipeline using Python for data collection and MySQL for storage, with Flask and ECharts for frontend visualization. Kabir et al. (2024) systematically reviewed Python’s capabilities across data cleaning, manipulation, and visualization, highlighting NumPy and Pandas as foundational libraries. Han and Kwak (2023) provided practical insights into Matplotlib and Seaborn, emphasizing their importance for exploratory data analysis and trend identification. Taleska et al. (2008), though foundational in nature, established the significance of SQL-based data preparation techniques — including views and star schemas — that continue to underpin modern visu-alization pipelines. Together, these studies confirm that Python and SQL work synergistically: SQL handles data extraction and pre-processing efficiently, while Python creates customized, interactive visualizations. This integration significantly enhances analytical ef-ficiency, reduces preprocessing time, and improves decision-making accuracy. The paper concludes that combining Python and SQL is essential for modern data visualization workflows, with future directions including real-time data integration and AI-assisted visu-alization.

title: Vibe Analysis: Exploring LLM Adoption by Data Visualization Practitioners
authors: Shani Claire Spivak; Aditi Krishna; Mahsan Nourani; Melanie K. Tory
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are enticing in their promise to support data visualization (Vis) through faster and simpler workflows for data prep, analysis, and visualization creation. Yet LLMs are notoriously error-prone and not built for data visualization tasks. Few studies have explored LLM adoption among Vis practitioners. To fill this gap, we conducted semi-structured interviews with members of the Data Visualization Society, a global community of data visualization designers. Our findings show that Vis designers actively use LLMs for both creative and technical aspects of the visualization process. A new visualization workflow is emerging, a process we call vibe analysis, analogous to vibe coding. Some key challenges raised by participants parallel those of vibe coding, while others are Vis-specific, like gaps in Vis knowledge and chart verification. This work opens up opportunities for research combining LLM-mediated work with Vis tools that incorporate data visualization guidance, constraints, and best practices.
venue: IEEE Computer Graphics and Applications

title: A systematic literature review of LLM-based data visualization
authors: Chiara Ceccarini; Paola Salomoni; Silvia Mirri; Giovanni Delnevo
abstract: The increasing popularity of Large Language Models (LLMs) has sparked growing interest in their application across a wide range of tasks, including data visualization. This study presents a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) aimed at investigating how LLMs are exploited to create data visualizations, addressing the research question: How can LLMs be used to create data visualizations? To this end, we identified ten dimensions of analysis, covering the study context, visualization-related aspects, and LLM-related characteristics. The visualization dimensions examine the types of visualizations produced, their outputs and interactivity, the underlying visualization theories or grammars, the intended target users, and the evaluation methodologies adopted. The remaining dimensions focus on the role and configuration of LLMs within the proposed approaches. Our findings provide a structured overview of current research trends, highlight how LLMs are currently leveraged to support or automate visualization creation, and identify open challenges and research gaps, offering directions for future work at the intersection of generative AI and data visualization.
venue: Discover Artificial Intelligence

title: Data Visualization improves Business Decision-Making.
authors: Sharvari More; Shreyash Patil; Needhumol Pillai
abstract: Abstract Organizations generate and collect large amount of data through their daily business activities.However ,raw data presentation in tables and numerical format it is difficult and time consuming for the managers to interpret the data.Data visualizations provides a better way to present the data in form of charts,graphs,dashboards and other visualization techniques which helps manager understand the patterns and trends more easily.There are more techniques like scatter charts,histograms and clustered charts etc,but we are mainly focusing on the particular four types of techniques. This research focuses on different data visualization techniques and identifying which visualization technique is more effective and useful for the decision-makers.The study will compare visualization techniques based on factors such as ease of understanding,ability to find trends and patterns and usefulness in decision-making.The study reviews existing literatures , and a practical comparison conducted using same business datasets represented through different visualization techniques.The study will identify strengths and limitations of each techniques and determine which techniques are more suitable for specific business information and decision-making requirements. Keywords: business decision-making,comparative study,data visualization,dashboards.

title: Evaluating the Impact of Data Visualization Professional Development on Early Childhood Educators
abstract: Many early childhood educators (ECE) lack confidence in using data visualization for classroom analysis, despite its effectiveness in making information accessible to young learners. This study examined whether a one-hour online professional development (PD) session could improve data visualization knowledge, self-efficacy, and implementation intentions among approximately 100 ECE participants. Using a pre-post quasi-experimental design with mixed methods, findings revealed a notable paradox, while technical knowledge remained stable, educators’ self-efficacy and implementation intentions increased significantly. Qualitative responses showed that educators view data visualization as a tool for inclusion that supports diverse learning styles and creates opportunities for all children to participate in mathematical thinking. This study aligns with the Texas Prekindergarten Guidelines (2022) and addresses the need for accessible, scalable PD for the Texas ECE workforce.
venue: Texas Educator Preparation

title: Using data visualizations for reading the word and the world
authors: Travis Weiland; Anita Sundrani; Shelton Shelton; Mandana Delavari
abstract: People are frequently exposed to a wide variety of data visualization in their daily lives. Though there is a long history of mathematics and statistics educators investigating ways to support people in reading graphs of data the demands of today’s diverse data visualizations are different and furthermore sociopolitical. In this paper we present the development process we went through to create a theory rich and empirical explored framework for reading data visualizations by investigating how teachers read data visualization in critical ways. We do this by presenting two iterations of a design research project aimed at developing mathematics teachers’ critical statistical literacy for doing and teaching data investigations of sociopolitical issues. From our two qualitative studies we found three meaningful conclusions: 1) What questions we ask in a data visualization activity seem to help create opportunities for people to read graphs in different ways. 2) How a data visualization relates to a person’s lived experience seems to impact how they read the data visualization. 3) Data visualization activities can serve as a starting point to developing critical statistical literacy connecting people’s current reading of the world with reading the word. Keywords: Statistics education; Data visualization; Critical literacy; Critical statistical ltieracy. Resumo As pessoas são frequentemente expostas a uma grande variedade de visualizações de dados em suas vidas diárias. Embora haja uma longa história de educadores de matemática e estatística investigando maneiras de ajudar as pessoas a ler gráficos de dados, as demandas das diversas visualizações de dados atuais são diferentes e, além disso, sociopolíticas. Neste artigo, apresentamos o processo de desenvolvimento pelo qual passamos para criar uma estrutura rica em teoria e explorada empiricamente para a leitura de visualizações de dados, investigando como os professores leem a visualização de dados de maneira crítica. Fazemos isso apresentando duas iterações de um projeto de pesquisa de design que visa desenvolver a alfabetização estatística crítica de professores de matemática para fazer e ensinar investigações de dados sobre questões sociopolíticas. A partir de nossos dois estudos qualitativos, chegamos a três conclusões significativas: 1) As perguntas que fazemos em uma atividade de visualização de dados parecem ajudar a criar oportunidades para as pessoas lerem gráficos de maneiras diferentes. 2) A forma como uma visualização de dados se relaciona com a experiência de vida de uma pessoa parece impactar a maneira como ela lê a visualização de dados. 3) As atividades de visualização de dados podem servir como ponto de partida para o desenvolvimento de uma alfabetização estatística crítica, conectando a leitura atual que as pessoas fazem do mundo com a leitura da palavra. Palavras-chave: Ensino de estatística; Visualização de dados; Alfabetização crítica; Alfabetização estatística crítica. Résumé Dans leur vie quotidienne, les gens sont fréquemment exposés à une grande variété de visualisations de données. Bien que les enseignants en mathématiques et en statistiques cherchent depuis longtemps des moyens d'aider les gens à lire les graphiques de données, les exigences actuelles en matière de visualisation de données sont différentes et, qui plus est, sociopolitiques. Dans cet article, nous présentons le processus de développement que nous avons suivi pour créer un cadre théorique et empirique riche pour la lecture des visualisations de données, en étudiant comment les enseignants lisent les visualisations de données de manière critique. Pour ce faire, nous présentons deux itérations d'un projet de recherche en conception visant à développer les compétences statistiques critiques des enseignants de mathématiques pour mener et enseigner des enquêtes sur des questions sociopolitiques à partir de données. Nos deux études qualitatives nous ont permis de tirer trois conclusions significatives : 1) Les questions que nous posons dans le cadre d'une activité de visualisation de données semblent contribuer à créer des occasions pour les gens de lire les graphiques de différentes manières. 2) La manière dont une visualisation de données est liée à l'expérience vécue d'une personne semble avoir un impact sur la façon dont elle lit la visualisation de données. 3) Les activités de visualisation des données peuvent servir de point de départ pour développer une culture statistique critique reliant la lecture actuelle du monde par les individus à la lecture du mot.

title: Data Visualization
abstract: Infographics are like glasses, says Alberto Cairo, who teaches data visualization at the University of Miami. If you take your glasses off, everything is blurry, but with your glasses on, everything comes into focus and makes sense. That analogy describes the impact of effective data visualizations. This chapter discusses various types of charts (such as pie, line and bar/column) and maps (including locator, thematic and symbol maps), and it explains how to know which type is right for your data. It includes Lena Groeger's “seeing” versus “thinking” framework for optimizing graphics for an audience. We then provide an overview of free tools for creating data visualizations, such as Infogram, Datawrapper, Flourish and Tableau. The chapter discusses how to choose the right colors, fonts and size for your graphic. Using Flourish, AI tools like Claude, Gemini, ChatGPT and NotebookLM with real-world data, we will walk through the process of making a variety of charts and maps. At the end of the chapter are exercises in which readers match datasets with the appropriate chart and map types. In addition, we point readers to various datasets and data visualization software to have them create data visualizations.

title: Less Is More? The Impact of Focusing Techniques on Recall Accuracy for Data Visualizations
abstract: Although visualization design guidelines commonly recommend using focusing techniques to guide viewers’ attention, the individual cognitive effects of color highlighting and annotation on recall remain unclear. Previous research has shown that focused visualizations can improve recall of emphasized information. However, it remains unclear whether this effect is driven by using color highlighting or annotation separately, or their combination, and whether focusing a visualization comes with a potential cost to recall of non-focused information. This study examined how color highlighting and annotation affect recall of focused and non-focused information in data visualizations. It was hypothesized that both color highlighting and annotation would lead to higher recall for focused information and lower recall for non-focused information, especially when combined. Participants ( N = 137) viewed eight data visualizations across four conditions: color highlighting, annotation, both techniques combined, and a decluttered design. The decluttered design served as a baseline condition without additional focusing cues. Participants answered cued free-response recall questions about both focused and non-focused information, and recall accuracy was measured as the percentage of correct answers. Results showed that both color highlighting and annotation led to higher recall accuracy for focused information. However, annotation was also associated with lower recall accuracy for non-focused information, whereas color highlighting had no significant effect. Combining the two techniques did not produce a stronger recall effect than using either technique alone. Overall, these findings support the use of focusing techniques in data visualizations, while suggesting that designers should consider the potential trade-offs of directing viewers’ attention.

title: Challenges and Opportunities for Theory-Grounded Data Visualization in Extended Reality
authors: Andreas Bueckle; Christiane V. R. Hütter; Renata G. Raidou; Chris Bryan; Peter Mindek; Hannes Kaufmann; Niklas Elmqvist; Jörg Menche; Katy Börner; Theresa-Marie Rhyne
abstract: Numerous frameworks have been developed for creating, interpreting, and teaching data visualizations. The past decade has seen advances in visualization paradigms beyond keyboard and mouse (e.g., immersive analytics). While mature visualization libraries exist for screen-based technologies, no comparable counterparts have emerged for immersive visualization due to scattered platforms, while theoretical frameworks require inclusion of extended reality (XR) and 3-D visualizations tailored to embodied exploration. Here, we synthesize challenges and opportunities for theory-grounded data visualization in XR to examine how established principles translate and expand to immersive environments. This work supports the development of both theory and practical tools for principled data visualization and exploration using XR in support of real-world applications.
venue: IEEE Computer Graphics and Applications

title: Data Visualization with ggplot2
abstract: In this chapter, we explore the power of data visualization in R, focusing on the ggplot2 package and its extensions. The ggplot2 package provides a graphical environment for creating a wide range of plots, from basic scatterplots to complex data visualizations. Through examples and practical tips, we examine the fundamental principles for producing custom data visualizations in R.

title: Modeling the adoption of AI-driven data visualization for service innovation in university libraries
authors: Khurshid Ahmad; Anas Alhur; Mehreen Azam; Salman Bin Naeem
abstract: Purpose The study examines the adoption of general-purpose generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools (e.g. ChatGPT, DeepSeek, Gemini) for data visualization tasks among academic librarians and its subsequent impact on library services innovation. Design/methodology/approach A quantitative research method was used, in which a cross-sectional survey on the extended model of the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) constructs was chosen in 100 universities of the Punjab province (both public and private sectors) in Pakistan with the help of a purposive sampling technique. Statistical Package for Social Sciences and Analysis of Moment Structure (SPSS-AMOS v-26) were applied to collect data and analyze it. Findings The findings of the study demonstrated that effort expectancy, social influence and facilitating conditions have a statistically significant influence on the behavioral intention to adopt GenAI tools for data visualization. Furthermore, the GenAI adoption has a significant positive impact on library service innovation. However, performance expectancy, hedonic motivation and price value have statistically insignificant impact on library professionals' behavioral intention to adopt GenAI tools. Originality/value This research provides original quantitative evidence from Pakistan, identifying the key factors influencing AI data visualization adoption in university libraries and its significant positive impact on service innovation.
venue: Reference Services Review

title: Data Visualization in Ukrainian Media: Typical Errors and Communicative Implications
abstract: The contemporary media landscape is characterised by a rapid increase in the volume of data analysed by journalists. At the same time, data visualization has become an integral tool for presenting information and shaping meaning in media publications. Large volumes of data can be transformed into a single static or dynamic visualization that is often more expressive than text. In this context, the quality of visual data representation in the media becomes particularly important, especially given the prevalence of common errors that affect the accuracy of data interpretation and the overall effectiveness of communication with mass audiences. The purpose of the study is to identify typical errors in data visualization in Ukrainian media and to determine their communicative implications. To achieve this aim, a set of methods was employed, including content analysis of media materials, the comparative-descriptive method, and elements of visual analysis. The empirical basis of the study consists of examples of data visualizations published in Ukrainian online media. The study identifies the main types of errors, including the incorrect use of color, visual clutter, inappropriate chart types, the absence of essential components (such as data sources, legends, and axis labels), and violations of scale and proportionality. Such errors complicate the process of information decoding, may lead to misinterpretation, reduce communication effectiveness, and undermine trust in media content. It is also emphasised that, in the digital environment, data visualizations can function as independent units of content, being disseminated across media platforms or social networks separately from the original text, often without additional clarification or explanation. This increases the importance of accurate and responsible graphical representation of data. The findings emphasise the importance of following basic information design principles and improving journalists’ visual literacy.
venue: Integrated communications

title: Optimizing Supply Chain Analytics with SAP S/4 HANA and Data Visualization Tools
abstract: Supply chain optimization is critical for achieving operational efficiency and reducing costs in today's competitive business environment. SAP S/4 HANA, an enterprise resource planning (ERP) software, offers advanced capabilities for integrating, analyzing, and improving supply chain processes. Combined with modern data visualization tools, businesses can extract actionable insights and enhance decision-making. This paper explores the integration of SAP S/4 HANA with data visualization platforms like Power BI and Tableau to address challenges such as demand forecasting, inventory management, and supplier performance analysis. By leveraging real-time data analytics and intuitive visual representations, organizations can achieve significant performance improvements in their supply chain operations.
venue: Global Journal of Innovative Research Perspectives (GJIRP)

title: Information Visualization for Hainan Li Pottery: An Intangible Cultural Heritage Perspective
abstract: Hainan Li pottery is a traditional pottery-making practice of the Li ethnic group in Hainan and contains information related to craft history, daily life, and cultural memory. At present, its communication mainly relies on object display, textual explanation, cultural experience activities, and tourism promotion. However, existing approaches often focus on individual objects and lack systematic presentation of historical development, production procedures, vessel types, decorative motifs, and cultural relationships. This study applies information visualization design to reorganize and represent the cultural information of Hainan Li pottery. Through literature review, exhibition observation, and visual material analysis, relevant information was classified into five aspects: historical development, cultural relationships, vessel types, production processes, and decorative motifs. Based on this classification, the Tao Qi Li Feng information visualization series was developed through visual elements, diagrams, and graphic structures. The study explores a design approach for transforming fragmented intangible cultural heritage information into a visual system. It provides a reference for the contemporary communication of Hainan Li pottery and other forms of traditional craftsmanship.
venue: Highlights in Art and Design

title: Visualize It: Designing Impactful and Accessible Data Visualizations
abstract: Data visualization is essential in library work, yet few practitioners receive formal training in it. This workshop equips library professionals at any level with a practical foundation in the design of accessible and effective data visualizations, combining theory with hands-on practice, leaving participants with a framework they can immediately apply.

title: Healthy skepticism in AI: a data visualization research agenda
authors: G. Elisabeta Marai; Marc Baaden; Michael Behrisch; Michael Krone; Pere‐Pau Vázquez
abstract: Research in data visualization of artificial intelligence (AI) models has historically focused on enhancing trust through visual explanations of AI. The trustworthiness line of work was built at least partially on an assumption that humans were critical users unlikely to adopt AI technology. It is increasingly clear that human trust levels in AI span, in fact, a wide range from critical to over-reliant. There is an urgent need to support both trust and healthy skepticism in AI solutions. We argue that it is healthy for humans to adopt a skeptical view both on the results of AI models and on the use of such AI models. We share our thoughts on the rising phenomenon of over-reliance on AI models, the risks and opportunities in using AI models, and the role of data visualization in over-reliance situations where humans are not motivated to engage in critical thinking.

title: Advanced Data Visualization Strategies for Communicating Complex Marketing Analytics to Executive Stakeholders
abstract: Advanced data visualization strategies are increasingly critical for communicating complex marketing analytics to executive stakeholders who require timely, accurate, and actionable insights. This study examines how sophisticated visualization techniques translate multidimensional marketing data into clear strategic narratives that support executive decision making. Drawing on contemporary literature in marketing analytics, information design, and executive cognition, the paper synthesizes best practices for visual abstraction, interactivity, and storytelling within dashboards and analytical reports. The study adopts a conceptual and analytical approach, reviewing empirical and practitioner-oriented studies on visualization use in executive environments. It evaluates visualization methods including interactive dashboards, heat maps, network graphs, temporal trend visualizations, and scenario-based simulations, emphasizing their suitability for summarizing performance metrics, forecasting outcomes, and communicating uncertainty. Findings indicate that well-designed visualizations significantly enhance comprehension, reduce cognitive overload, and improve alignment between marketing teams and executive leadership. By integrating key performance indicators with contextual annotations and drill-down capabilities, visualization tools enable executives to move beyond descriptive metrics toward strategic interpretation. The paper further explores the role of automation, artificial intelligence, and real-time data pipelines in supporting adaptive visualization systems. These systems allow dynamic updates, personalized executive views, and rapid comparison across channels, segments, and time horizons. Importantly, the study highlights common pitfalls, including misleading visual encodings, excessive complexity, and misalignment with executive information needs. Ethical considerations such as data integrity, transparency, and responsible representation of uncertainty are also examined, underscoring the need for governance standards in executive reporting. Overall, the study proposes a practical framework for advanced data visualization in marketing analytics that balances analytical rigor with executive usability. The framework emphasizes clarity, relevance, and narrative coherence as central design principles. By adopting these strategies, organizations can improve strategic communication, accelerate evidence-based decision-making, and enhance the perceived value of marketing analytics at the executive level. The paper contributes actionable guidance for practitioners and establishes a foundation for future empirical research on visualization effectiveness, executive cognition, and strategic analytics communication in increasingly data driven organizational environments. These insights are particularly relevant for multinational firms, digital platforms, and public organizations navigating complexity, accountability, and strategic transformation under persistent uncertainty in competitive global markets.
venue: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF MARKETING AND COMMUNICATION STUDIES

title: Spaciousness and Style: Finding Old Rhetoric in Data Visualizations
abstract: This article revisits Richard Weaver’s concept of spaciousness as a rhetorical effect and repositions it within contemporary visual rhetoric, particularly data visualizations. Although Weaver’s account of spaciousness is rooted in a political ideology that presumes shared cultural values, the concept offers a useful lens for understanding how style operates in visual communication. Drawing on the classical Ciceronian styles, this article argues that spaciousness functions as a visual analogue of the grand style, emphasizing abstraction rather than detail. Analyses of sparklines, cartographic maps, network visualizations, and metaphor-based displays show how plain style prioritizes instruction and transparency, grand style cultivates openness and shared meaning, and middle style modulates between visual scales through perceptual or interactive zooming. The article demonstrates how stylistic spaciousness in data visualization reinforces cultural assumptions about connectivity, complexity, and knowledge, offering a rhetorically grounded approach to studying visual style.
venue: Rhetoric Review

title: Data Visualization Tools and Techniques
abstract: This research paper provides an overview of Data Visualization Tools and Techniques and examines their role in Business Analytics and data-driven decision-making. It explains how large and complex datasets can be transformed into clear and meaningful visual representations that help analysts and decision-makers identify patterns, trends, relationships, and important business information. The study discusses commonly used data visualization techniques, including line plots, bar charts, pie and donut charts, histograms, scatter plots, box-and-whisker plots, and network diagrams. It also reviews several widely used visualization tools, including Tableau, Dundas BI, Jupyter, Google Charts, IBM Watson, and Microsoft Power BI, highlighting their capabilities and applications in handling, analyzing, and presenting data. The paper further explores the importance of visualization in business environments, particularly for dashboards, reports, sales and marketing analysis, investor presentations, and other decision-support activities. Overall, the research demonstrates how appropriate visualization techniques and tools can make complex data easier to understand, improve the communication of analytical insights, and support more informed business decisions.

title: Impact of Tableau Data Visualization on Business Decision-Making
authors: Vaishnavi Chavan and Dr. Kiran Tikar
abstract: Data has become an important resource for modern businesses, as organizations generate large volumes of information through sales, customer activities, finance, marketing, and operations. However, raw data is often difficult to interpret and use effectively for business decisions. Data visualization helps address this problem by presenting complex information through charts, graphs, and interactive dashboards. Tableau is a widely used business intelligence and visualization platform that allows users to explore data, identify trends, monitor performance, and generate business insights. This paper examines the impact of Tableau data visualization on business decision-making, with particular emphasis on interactive dashboards, filters, charts, drill-down analysis, and visual exploration. The study follows a descriptive and analytical approach and is based on secondary information obtained from academic publications and other credible research sources. Greater emphasis is given to studies published in 2024 and 2025 to reflect recent developments in dashboard-based decision support and Tableau applications. The reviewed literature suggests that well-designed dashboards can improve information understanding, reduce task complexity, support performance analysis, and assist managers in making timely and informed decisions. Recent Tableau-related research also shows the practical value of interactive dashboards for sales analysis in MSMEs. Overall, Tableau can support business decision-making when reliable data, suitable visualization design, relevant business context, and user skills are considered together
venue: International Journal of Advanced Research in Science Communication and Technology

title: Creating Understandable Data Visualizations in R
abstract: Data visualization is central to scientific communication, yet many clinicians and early-career researchers struggle to create clear and interpretable figures.This article presents a beginner-friendly approach to building charts in R using the grammar of graphics framework.Every element of a chart is a choice, and the default is rarely the best one.Using a simulated clinical dataset of systolic blood pressure across treatment groups, we demonstrate how plots are constructed explicitly by combining data, aesthetic mappings, and geometric representations.Through stepby-step examples, we show how deliberate layering of axis labels, titles, color palettes, and themes transforms a bare-minimum plot into a publication-ready figure.By emphasizing deliberate decision-making over reliance on software defaults, this work aims to lower barriers to effective data visualization and support transparent scientific reporting.
venue: Journal of Postgraduate Medicine Education and Research

title: Data Visualization
authors: Megan Shields Formato; Kevin C. Moore; Sarah Peterson Pittock; Emily Polk; Cassie A. Wright
abstract: This chapter introduces data visualization as a central practice in science communication, showing how well-designed charts translate complex evidence into clear visual insights for diverse audiences. It traces the evolution of visualization from early tabular records and cartography through Enlightenment statistical graphics, nineteenth-century public health maps, and modern interactive and AI-supported visualizations, demonstrating how graphics have shaped scientific reasoning and public decision-making throughout history. It then presents core principles for effective chart design: understanding audience and purpose, visual and statistical integrity, appropriate chart types, and designing with an eye toward decluttering, visual hierarchy, and contextual annotation to support accurate viewer interpretation. As with other chapters in this book, it also examines how emerging technologies and AI tools are transforming data visualization while emphasizing the continued importance of human judgment, ethics, and credibility. Emphasizing visualization as a rhetorical act, this chapter explains how effective charts communicate arguments, not just data. This chapter concludes with a practical process—from defining a “big idea” to sketching, feedback, prototyping, and refinement—equipping readers with strategies and tools to create ethical and effective visualizations.

title: Analysis of the Dissemination Path of Marxist Classical Theory Based on Data Visualization Technology
authors: S. Q. Wang; X. X. Wu
abstract: This study applies data visualization technology to analyze the dissemination paths of Marxist classical theory within complex social networks. Integrating communication theory, social network analysis, and visualization techniques, the research constructs a multidimensional analytical framework to examine how Marxist theory propagates across different network structures. Based on simulation experiments involving diverse audience groups and dissemination channels, the study identifies the differentiated roles of academic, political, and mass media nodes in shaping propagation speed, coverage, and influence. The results show that scale-free networks generally exhibit faster earlystage diffusion and higher overall coverage under hub-dominated conditions, while small-world networks may achieve comparable or superior early propagation speed when initial propagators are embedded in highly clustered communities. These findings highlight the conditional effects of network topology and node roles on ideological dissemination. The study demonstrates the value of data visualization in revealing structural mechanisms of theory diffusion and provides methodological reference for network propagation analysis, information-flow modeling, and signal-diffusion studies in complex communication environments.
venue: Advanced Electromagnetics

title: Lumi Liu on Data Visualization, Medical Communication, and the Art of Making Complexity Clear
abstract: This interview documents the professional journey of Lumi Liu, focusing on the intersection of branding, data visualization, and scientific storytelling. The text explores the methodology of translating complex medical and technical information into clear, emotionally resonant visual narratives, analyzes the balance between artistic expression and scientific accuracy in medical illustration, and investigates the evolving role of the designer as a communicator across cultures and disciplines. As part of Curatone.art's research project, we feature Lumi Liu — a distinguished creative designer, art director, and co-founder of ING Studio. This interview explores how the synergy between rigorous data visualization and compelling visual storytelling defines the role of the contemporary communication designer in the 21st century.

title: Application of Topic Modeling and Data Visualization in Libraries: A Review of Literature
abstract: This study explores the evolving role of topic modeling and data visualization within Library and Information Science (LIS), focusing on their theoretical underpinnings, practical applications, and recent research trends. To clearly understand the techniques, 73 scholarly publications, published between 2003 24, were retrieved from different databases such as Scopus, Web of Science, LISA, and Google Scholar. A detailed review of the literature of the publications was done to understand the theoretical aspects of the techniques and their prospects. Topic modeling is a sophisticated text-mining technique that can be done using a variety of algorithms such as LDA, STM etc., each one suited to different types of datasets and research objectives, with diverse applications in libraries such as Enhancing Information Retrieval and Search Systems, Improving Digital Library Services, Document Clustering and Recommendation Systems, Subject Metadata and Multimedia Libraries, Topic Trends and Knowledge Discovery in LIS etc. Analytical findings of the publications reveal that 75% of the literature emerged in the past decade, with a notable concentration between 2018 and 2022, indicating heightened academic interest in these data-driven methodologies. The reviewed documents include journal articles (70%), conference papers (18%), book chapters (9%), and theses (3%), highlighting diverse scholarly contributions. Topic modeling techniques, particularly Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA), are recognized for uncovering hidden patterns in large text corpora, while data visualization translates complex datasets into impactful visuals. Together, these tools offer immense value to LIS professionals, data analysts, and researchers seeking to advance knowledge discovery, improve decision-making, and enhance scholarly communication in modern libraries

title: The Science and Art of Data Visualization
abstract: Before starting on the creation of graphs, this chapter discusses basic concepts of data visualization, as well as strategies for managing and organizing information in a structured way. Then, the choice of appropriate graphics according to human visual perception is explored, with emphasis on Gestalt principles and pre-attentive attributes. Finally, useful tools for data visualization are described.

title: Words as Data: Integrating Data Visualizations and English Language Arts for Classrooms with Multilingual Students
authors: Victor R. Lee; Elizabeth Finlayson Harris; Ruishi Chen; Sarah R. Levine
abstract: :This paper presents findings from a design-based research project that integrates quantitative text analytics data visualizations into middle school English Language Arts (ELA) classrooms, with particular attention to multilingual learners. In collaboration with a public school district, we co-designed data visualizations (e.g., word clouds, word frequency graphs) and instructional routines to support literary engagement and text comprehension using quantitative features of text. Drawing on survey data and classroom video excerpts, we examined how students engaged with these materials and how their perceptions of reading and data work changed. Participating teachers aided in visualization and routine design and implemented visualization use at least three times in their classroom. A control group of teachers proceeded with existing curriculum and activities. Compared to a control group, students who participated in these activities—especially those still developing English proficiency—showed more positive shifts in attitudes toward reading and working with data. These findings suggest that lightweight data integrations in ELA can support students' interpretive practices that are emphasized in ELA classrooms while also promoting data literacy, particularly for linguistically diverse populations.

title: DATA ANALYTICS AND DATA VISUALIZATION
abstract: Data Analytics and Data Visualization is a comprehensive resource designed to help readers understand the principles, methodologies, and tools used to transform raw data into meaningful insights. In today's data-driven world, organizations across industries rely on data analytics and visualization techniques to make informed decisions, identify trends, improve performance, and gain a competitive advantage. This book provides a structured approach to learning the concepts and practical applications of data analytics, statistical analysis, predictive modeling, and business intelligence. The book begins by introducing the fundamentals of data analytics, including the importance of data, different types of analytics, and the roles of data professionals. It then explores essential statistical concepts and Python fundamentals that form the basis for data analysis. Readers gain an understanding of probability theory, hypothesis testing, sampling techniques, and statistical methods commonly used in analytical decision-making. Further, the book covers predictive analytics techniques such as regression, classification, and clustering, enabling readers to uncover patterns and make data-driven predictions. The final section focuses on data visualization using Power BI, one of the most widely used business intelligence platforms. Topics include data transformation, modeling, dashboard development, and report sharing for effective communication of insights. Combining theoretical concepts with practical applications, this book is ideal for students, researchers, business professionals, analysts, and aspiring data scientists. It serves as a valuable guide for developing analytical thinking and visualization skills necessary for success in the modern data economy.

title: Technology Integration in Community Service: Empowering IDX Employees with Data Visualization Skills
authors: Wirda Andani; Hendra Perdana; Nurfitri Imro’ah; Evy Sulistianingsih; Neva Satyahadewi; Ray Tamtama; Shantika Martha; Yuyun Eka Pratiwi; Pitriani Pitriani; Annisa Auliarahmi; Muhammad Fikri
abstract: Background: The rapid growth of digitalization in the capital market requires the Indonesia Stock Exchange (IDX) to deliver transparent, accurate, and understandable information through data visualization. However, employees at the IDX West Kalimantan Representative Office rarely process and visualize data, even though it is essential for carrying out daily tasks. Contribution: This study fills the gap in technology-based community service programs that rarely integrate infographic training with information literacy enhancement in capital market education. The novelty of this study lies in the evaluation of the community service program, which not only measures the effectiveness of the training but also employs CB-SEM to identify the factors influencing participants’ learning outcomes. Method: The Statistics Study Program, Untan, conducted a training workshop combining theory and practice with real data. A situational analysis with IDX representatives was first carried out to identify needs and design the program. Effectiveness was evaluated using pre-tests, post-tests, and satisfaction surveys. Results: The paired t-test results at the 5% significance level demonstrating the effectiveness of infographic training in enhancing data visualization skills. In addition, CB-SEM analysis revealed that the module variable was the dominant factor, highlighting the importance of structured and relevant training materials in supporting participants’ learning outcomes. Conclusion: The training effectively enhanced the knowledge and skills of IDX West Kalimantan Representative employees in data processing and visualization.

abstract: Today, the brand new digital economy has revolutionized the way people travel and find a place to stay through platforms like Airbnb. For this purpose, this project is dedicated to delving into Airbnb data with the help of efficient data visualization methods to reveal significant patterns and insights. The study, by analyzing various factors such as pricing location types of rooms, availability, and customer reviews, is aiming at finding the answer to how different variables affect listing performance and user preferences. Through the use of visualization software, not only are complex datasets opened up in a simple and interactive visual manner like charts, graphs, and maps but it also becomes much easier to recognize the patterns and associations. title: Future of AI Jobs: A Data Visualization Analysis Using Tableau
authors: Diana Moses; Prateek Dhamangave; Omair Mohiuddin
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming the global employment landscape by influencing job roles, skill requirements, salary structures, and workforce demand. Understanding these changes requires effective analytical techniques capable of extracting meaningful insights from complex labor market datasets. This study presents a comprehensive data visualization analysis of an AI employment dataset using Tableau. The dataset contains information related to job roles, salary ranges, skill demand scores, geographic distribution, and employment characteristics. Various visualization techniques including bar charts, heat maps, histograms, funnel charts, and geographic analyses were employed to identify patterns and trends within the AI labor market. The analysis reveals significant differences in salary distribution across countries, varying levels of AI automation risk among job roles, increasing skill demand over time, and strong global demand for technical professionals. The findings demonstrate that while automation affects certain occupations, highly specialized roles continue to remain resilient due to the need for advanced problem-solving and domain expertise. The study highlights the effectiveness of Tableau as a business intelligence and visualization platform for transforming raw employment data into actionable insights. The results provide valuable information for students, professionals, recruiters, and policymakers seeking to understand emerging workforce trends in the era of Artificial Intelligence. title: grapesDraw : Bridging Data Visualization for Statistical Education and Research in Agriculture
authors: Burra Preeti; Pratheesh Pradeep Gopinath; V. S. Adarsh; Blesson B. Varghese; Mohammed Hisham M; Manju Mary Paul
abstract: Data visualization is pivotal in agricultural research, yet tools like R, Python, and Excel pose significant challenges. R's advanced graphics are offset by a steep learning curve, Python often encounters runtime errors, and Excel lacks robust functionality. To overcome these obstacles, we introduce grapesDraw, an open‐source web application, and R package tailored for agricultural research and education. Built on Shiny, grapesDraw integrates R's ggplot2, corrplot, packcircles, and factoextra packages, offering an intuitive interface that minimizes coding demands. This enables researchers and students to create high‐quality visualizations effortlessly. A survey across state agricultural universities (SAUs) confirmed grapesDraw's usability and effectiveness, particularly among novices. Freely available on shinyapps.io and as an R package on GitHub, with detailed documentation, grapesDraw enhances accessibility and efficiency in agricultural data visualization.

title: Data visualization and visual analytics as support for the investigation of document and identity fraud in the public sector
abstract: Verifying citizens' identities and the authenticity of documents has become a critical step in the delivery of public services, especially with the expansion of digital government and the growth of identity fraud attempts in Brazil. Much of this verification still depends on the comparison of images and records by human analysts, a task that cognitive psychology research shows to be subject to relevant error rates. This article analyzes the role of data visualization and visual analytics tools as support for the investigation of document and identity fraud in the public sector. It is a qualitative and exploratory study, based on bibliographic and documentary research, combining work on information visualization, unfamiliar face matching, cognitive load theory, visual analytics applied to fraud detection and the interaction between humans and automated systems in public administration. The analysis indicates that interfaces able to gather evidence in a single environment, support side-by-side comparison and reduce switching between systems tend to lower cognitive effort and may favor more consistent decisions. The literature also shows that combining a trained specialist with a highperforming algorithm outperforms the combination of two specialists, while warning about algorithmic bias, automation bias and harms already observed in public anti-fraud programs. The study concludes that visualization should be conceived as an instrument that amplifies human judgment, with traceable decisions and safeguards for citizens' rights.

title: Enhancing Project Management Performance Through Data Visualization Using Microsoft Power BI
abstract: Effective project management requires continuous monitoring of schedules, budgets, resources, and project deliverables. However, organizations often collect project information from multiple sources, making it difficult for managers to obtain a clear understanding of overall project performance. Traditional reporting methods, particularly manually maintained spreadsheets and static reports, can delay the identification of project problems and limit informed decision-making. This research examines the role of data visualization and business intelligence in improving project management through Microsoft Power BI. A conceptual framework is proposed to integrate project information, transform raw data, calculate key performance indicators (KPIs), and present results through interactive dashboards. The framework focuses on project completion, schedule variance, cost variance, budget utilization, resource allocation, and risk monitoring. A literature-based research methodology is adopted to examine existing studies on project success, performance measurement, business intelligence, and dashboard visualization. The proposed approach demonstrates how Power BI can provide a centralized reporting environment and improve the accessibility and interpretation of project information. The study concludes that integrating business intelligence with project management can support transparency, performance monitoring, and evidence-based decisions, provided that the underlying data is accurate and regularly updated.

title: Basketball Game Data Visualization and Prediction Model Based on Voting Ensemble Learning
abstract: Aiming at the insufficient visualization effect of basketball game data, this paper proposes a mixed prediction model based on voting ensemble learning and improved random forest. The experiment showed that the average accuracy of the model reached 0.856, the average absolute error was stable within 0.021-0.041, and the response time of real-time event data visualization was less than 0.8 seconds. The core innovation of the research method is to propose a cluster optimization algorithm to solve the inefficient classification of unlabeled data in traditional random forests. A mixed voting strategy is designed, where hard voting is used for discrete event classification and soft voting is used for continuous index prediction to enhance the model generalization ability of complex event scenarios.

title: PlotCraft: Pushing the Limits of LLMs for Complex and Interactive Data Visualization
authors: Zhang, Jiajun; Zhang, Jianke; Cui, Zeyu; Yang, Jiaxi; Zhang, Lei; Hui, Binyuan; Liu, Qiang; Wang, Zilei; Wang, Liang; Lin, Junyang
abstract: Recent Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable proficiency in code generation. However, their ability to create complex visualizations for scaled and structured data remains largely unevaluated and underdeveloped. To address this gap, we introduce PlotCraft, a new benchmark featuring 1k challenging visualization tasks that cover a wide range of topics, such as finance, scientific research, and sociology. The benchmark is structured around seven high-level visualization tasks and encompasses 48 distinct chart types. Crucially, it is the first to systematically evaluate both single-turn generation and multi-turn refinement across a diverse spectrum of task complexities. Our comprehensive evaluation of 23 leading LLMs on PlotCraft reveals obvious performance deficiencies in handling sophisticated visualization tasks. To bridge this performance gap, we develope SynthVis-30K, a large-scale, high-quality dataset of complex visualization code synthesized via a collaborative agent framework. Building upon this dataset, we develope PlotCraftor, a novel code generation model that achieves strong capabilities in complex data visualization with a remarkably small size. Across VisEval, PandasPlotBench, and our proposed PlotCraft, PlotCraftor shows performance comparable to that of leading proprietary approaches. Especially, on hard task, Our model achieves over 50% performance improvement. We will release the benchmark, dataset, and code at https://github.com/Speakn0w/PlotCraft-Benchmark.

title: MakeMyFigure: An Interactive Platform for Reproducible Quantitative Data Visualization, Analysis, and Scientific Figure Construction
authors: Suresh Poudel; Him K. Shrestha; Jeremy C. Crawford; Fabio Demontis; Douglas R. Green
abstract: Reproducible data analysis and visualization are essential for reliable biological and biomedical research, yet creating high-quality, publication-ready figures often requires moving data and results between multiple analysis, visualization, and graphics tools. This fragmented, multi-layered process can make it difficult to trace how individual figure panels were generated, preserve the underlying analytical decisions, and reproduce them later. Here, we introduce MakeMyFigure, a free and open-source platform for data visualization, analysis, and creation of multi-panel scientific figures. MakeMyFigure integrates data processing, statistical analysis, visualization, and figure assembly within a single workflow. It supports a range of quantitative data formats and structures, including feature-by-sample matrices and precomputed statistical results, and provides data-aware visualization recommendations to help users select appropriate plots from a library of 38 visualization types. These capabilities allow researchers to move directly from experimental measurements to commonly used statistical analyses and graphical representations without requiring programming expertise. Eighteen statistical procedures are implemented, and their results are drawn directly onto the plot families that support statistical annotation, keeping analytical results linked to the panels they generate. Importantly, MakeMyFigure uses machine-readable JSON specifications to record the identity and checksum of the source data, the processing steps, visualization settings, and statistical parameters used to generate each figure panel. It can also save a figure as a portable package, freezing the specifications together with the data. This allows figures to be regenerated from their recorded specifications and source data, or from the package alone on another computer, rather than relying on manually reconstructed workflows. Using published datasets from several biological fields, independent statistical validation in R, and a comparison with 15 representative analysis, visualization, and figure-generation tools, we show that MakeMyFigure combines accessible, code-free figure creation with panel-level computational reproducibility. Overall, MakeMyFigure provides a unified approach for creating, documenting, and reproducing scientific figures. Source code and documentation are available at https://github.com/surPoudel/make-my-figure , https://github.com/surPoudel/make-my-figure/releases/tag/v1.1.0 .

title: DIGITAL DATA VISUALIZATION & INFORMATION SYSTEMS Date-of-Birth Graphical Signature
abstract: This article proposes DOB-GS, a new graphical and mathematical method for representing a Date of Birth (DOB) as a distinctive numerical profile. In the proposed method, a DOB in DD-MM-YYYY format is converted into an eight-digit sequence, with each digit plotted on a vertical scale from 0 to 9 according to its sequential position. The eight points are connected to form a DOB Graph, producing a visual representation of the digit structure of the date. Mathematical parameters including Total Graph Movement (TGM), Maximum Digit Jump (MDJ), Digit Range (DR), upward/downward transitions, horizontal transitions, and a checksum can be derived from the graph. The resulting numerical signature may be associated with a digitally signed QR Code for document-data consistency checking and could potentially be investigated for use in digital certificates and identity/document-verification systems. The proposal is intended as a data-visualization and computational representation technique, not as a method for predicting personality, health, behavior, or destiny.

title: Review of Data Visualization Applications in Activity Reports of Istanbul District Municipalities
abstract: Our age has resolved critical actions in managerial processes such as storage and retention of data, creating a huge pile of data whose processing and visualization has become valuable for making sense of and expressing it. Visualization provides a powerful representation to extract meaning and discover insights from data, strengthening the narrative that institutions and organizations use in their reports. However, this is not as straightforward as it may seem: visualization is difficult to use and complex to implement, and when applied incorrectly, it creates greater complexity and makes the story it tells multi-layered. Visualization therefore needs to be faithful to its context and appropriate for its target audience, taking the data-to-ink ratio into account. Within the scope of this study, the data visualization techniques used in the most recent (2024) annual activity reports of the district municipalities of Istanbul, published as open access, were identified and classified through a mixed-methods design combining document analysis and content analysis. A total of 9,742 pages across the reports of 39 municipalities were reviewed (Şile Municipality was excluded, as its 2024 report was unavailable), and the chart types and features used were coded by dual coders with over 90% agreement. The findings indicate that municipalities predominantly rely on basic-level visualizations, particularly first-level chart types such as bar, line, and pie charts, and that tables are largely transferred into reports without formatting or customization. A low data-to-ink ratio, frequent use of three-dimensional and decorative chart elements, and limited use of spatial mapping and interactive presentation techniques were also observed. Errors in the preferred visualization formats and chart types were identified when evaluated against universal design principles. This study is important for examining and evaluating visualization techniques in the annual reports of public institutions, offering a baseline for improving the accessibility and communicative effectiveness of municipal reporting practices.

title: Beyond Exploration: AI-facilitated Information Visualization Structure for Complex Context Exploration and Decision-Making in Environmental Sustainability
authors: Qiming Sun; I‐Han Hsiao; Shih-Yi James Chien
abstract: Institutional sustainability campaigns often rely on static “playbooks” to disseminate pro-environmental advice. These linear, text-heavy resources are difficult to navigate when users must compare actions across effort, impact, and personal relevance. We investigate how different information visualization structures shape sustainability planning by comparing three interfaces: an AI-enhanced List, Quadrants, and an Interactive Map. The interfaces share a hybrid content pipeline in which sustainability practices are curated by human experts and enriched with LLM-generated metadata for visualization. In a within-subjects study with 115 university-affiliated participants, we found no significant differences in adoption volume or perceived discovery across interfaces. However, interface structure substantially affected workload and decision quality. The Map imposed significantly higher mental demand, frustration, and effort than both structured alternatives, lowered decision confidence, and was rated as less helpful than the institution’s original playbook. Quadrants emerged as the most preferred interface in post-study rankings, suggesting that lightweight semantic grouping can support exploration without the cognitive cost of free-form spatial navigation. These findings refine the design of AI-enhanced decision support tools for personal sustainability and other multi-criteria personal informatics domains.

title: An Eye-Tracking-Based Evaluation Model for Information Visualization Design Effectiveness
authors: Na Wang; Weiqian Mao; Shengnan Wu; Jiahui Wang
abstract: This study proposes an eye-tracking-based model to assess information visualization effectiveness. By integrating eye movement metrics—First Fixation Duration (FFD), Total Fixation Duration (TFD), Scanpath Length, and Entropy—with task performance (Accuracy Rate), a composite index termed Visualization Effectiveness Index (VEI) is constructed. A controlled experiment with expert and novice users across multiple visualization types (tree diagrams, heatmaps, and Sankey diagrams) shows that the model effectively differentiates design approaches and provides insights into visual efficiency, cognitive load, and user comprehension. Compared with traditional subjective methods, it improves reliability and reproducibility and supports data-driven visualization design optimization.

title: What Cognitive Accessibility Reveals About Data Visualization
authors: Keke Wu; Jinjuan Heidi Feng; Jonathan K. Lazar
abstract: Data visualization aims to augment human cognition and make data accessible to diverse audiences. As data increasingly shapes participation and decision-making across many domains, there is a growing need to examine whether prevailing assumptions in visualization adequately reflect the diversity of human abilities, experiences, and needs. We argue that cognitive accessibility provides a critical lens for examining these questions and functions as a stress test for visualization theory. Drawing on cognitive accessibility research and our experiences studying accessible visualization, we identify three interconnected assumptions that shape visualization research and practice: assumptions about what forms of cognition visualization supports, how accessibility is defined and measured, and whose needs and abilities are centered in design and evaluation. Making these assumptions explicit reveals opportunities to rethink longstanding approaches and open new directions. Ultimately, we believe that cognitive accessibility can serve as a catalyst for innovation, expanding what visualization supports, whom it serves, and the roles it plays in people's lives.

title: ManyFold: A Design Exploration of Data Visualization on Foldable Mobile Devices
authors: Julian Baader; Ricardo Langner; Can Liu; Raimund Dachselt
abstract: With this work, we explore the unique potential of data visualization on novel foldable mobile devices (foldables). Even though foldables are already commercially available, there is limited knowledge of how to leverage their distinct characteristics for visualization. This gap will only grow as their form factors become increasingly diverse. To address this, we use a two-step approach. First, we present a device-centered design space, structured around physical and usage properties of foldable devices. Second, we introduce a conceptual framework that investigates visualization on foldables from four complementary perspectives: More Displays - distributing multiple views to leverage additional display space; More Shapes - mapping visualizations to spatial fold states; More Interactions - coupling visualization tasks and folding interactions; and More States - enabling responsive visualization through folding. We complement the design space and conceptual framework with a low-fidelity ideation workshop and the subsequent prototyping of interactive artifacts. We reflect on the results and lessons learned from our exploratory, design-driven process and discuss opportunities and challenges, including the gap between our proposed concepts and commercially available foldable devices. By providing conceptual foundations and illustrating the potential of foldables, we hope to inspire and inform the development of future visualization applications for this evolving class of devices.

title: Harness Engineering for Multi-Agent Data Visualization with Small Language Models
authors: Peilin Wang; Xinxiao Li; Eisei Nakahara
abstract: Turning a natural-language question into a correct, publication-ready data visualization usually takes several rounds of coding, inspection, and debugging. Large language models can draft plotting code, but a single-shot model call has no way to run the code, look at the resulting image, recover from execution errors, or decide whether the chart actually answers the user. We demonstrate a visualization harness: an engineered scaffold that wraps a team of seven specialized agents in a bounded Plan–Execute–Verify–Refine control loop. The harness, not any single model, supplies the capabilities that make the system reliable—a sandboxed execution environment with timeouts, vision-based verification of the rendered PNG, error-driven routing between re-planning, re-coding and debugging, per-agent model assignment, and persistent run state for resume and reproducibility. Because the harness owns reliability, the underlying models can be small: a hybrid configuration that runs four agents on local small language models (3–8B) and routes only the three failure-prone agents to inexpensive cloud models reaches a 100% verification pass rate across five heterogeneous datasets at roughly one-third the cost of an all-cloud baseline. The live demo, built on a lightweight FastAPI web UI, lets attendees upload a dataset, type a query, and watch agent steps and intermediate charts stream in real time over Server-Sent Events until a verified visualization appears.

title: An Algorithmic Perspective on Information Visualization
abstract: Information visualization is inherently a field that brings together various research domains. Roughly speaking, we may identify two perspectives: the design perspective, revolving around how to ensure that a human can work effectively with the visual representations of data and the tools that offer them, and the algorithmic perspective, focusing on how to automatically create such visual representations. Munzner's model for visualization design places design choices before algorithmic considerations. It offers predominantly a design perspective; as a consequence, applications of this model may consider the algorithmic perspective as an afterthought, bypassing a step that translates the design into the formalism necessary for algorithmic study. As a result, the design may be entangled with the algorithms used to compute a visualization. Focusing on layout algorithms, we explore the ramifications of this entanglement: quality often goes undefined and unmeasured, and ad-hoc heuristics tend to be applied, reducing trustworthiness and potentially leading to incorrect conclusions. We look at how we may complement Munzner's model---the design perspective---with a clear model of the algorithmic perspective, to obtain a formal, measured understanding of the interplay between visualizations and the algorithms used to create them. Paradoxically, the solution lies in a clearer separation of concerns between design and algorithm. We argue that this model leads to better comparison between approaches, a more fine-grained understanding of their strengths and weaknesses, and allows for uncovering new opportunities, as to eventually lead to a better understanding of visualization.

abstract: Under the indigenously developed hardware and software environment, this paper designs and implements an environment situational information visualization system based on a hierarchical architecture and efficient graphic control capabilities. The system aims to address challenges such as massive data volumes, low rendering efficiency, and inadequate software architecture, thereby meeting the stringent visualization requirements for multi-source heterogeneous data on domestic platforms. By visualizing multi-source heterogeneous information on a 2D/3D digital map, the system demonstrates high practical value. It provides accurate and clear environment situational information for field personnel, laying a solid foundation for informed decision-making in digitalized operations.

However, the lack of knowledge and skills of teachers at the Fajrul Karim Islamic Boarding School in operating Excel is a major obstacle. Data visualization is one method of conveying information studied in statistics. The Excel training provided aims to provide an understanding regarding the application of statistical methods with Excel and its visualization so that teachers at the Fajrul Karim Serang Banten Islamic boarding school can better understand student grades. title: Interactive Mascot: A Scene-Centric Interaction Grammar for Data Visualizations
abstract: Scene-centric visualization systems expose semantic components, such as marks, encodings, layouts, and axes, as first-class objects that can be directly manipulated. Existing interaction abstractions, however, are largely based on event streams, signals, and data selections rather than semantic scene components. This mismatch makes interactions involving scene components less natural to specify and limits the expressive power of scene-centric visualization systems. We present Interactive Mascot, a scene-centric interaction grammar for data visualizations. Interactive Mascot extends scene-centric representations for static visualizations by modeling interactive behavior as information flow among four interaction components (trigger, responder, evaluator, and updater) and two forms of context (event context and state context). To realize these semantics, we introduce a dependency-graph execution model that systematically transforms interaction specifications into executable dependency graphs using reusable graph patterns associated with semantic visualization components. We implement Interactive Mascot in the JavaScript library Mascot$.$js and evaluate its performance and usability. Interactive Mascot achieves runtime performance comparable to Vega-Lite, and a qualitative user study shows that the grammar is learnable and usable for interaction authoring.

title: A Qualitative Analysis of Prompt Engineering for Data Visualization
authors: Camile Maria Cunha Aguiar; Walbert Cunha Monteiro; Thiago Augusto Soares de Sousa; Aruanda Simões Gonçalves Meiguins; Roberto Yuri da Silva Franco; Bianchi Serique Meiguins
abstract: There is limited understanding of how different prompt construction techniques affect the clarity and interpretation of instructions for creating data visualizations. This article investigates the influence of the following prompt engineering techniques, applied to the interaction between users and ChatGPT Go 5.2: zero-shot, few-shot, and Visualization Query Language (VQL). We conducted a qualitative study, employing Direct Content Analysis to assess structural completeness and Reflective Thematic Analysis to identify recurring patterns and themes in the prompts. Our results demonstrated that structured techniques, such as VQL and hybrid approaches, improve the structure and objectivity of prompts but can not eliminate semantic ambiguity, particularly in data transformations and aggregations. We also indicated a persistent non-deterministic behavior in the model, in which semantically equivalent prompts frequently generate inconsistent visualizations. These findings provide a qualitative characterization of the engineering challenges of prompts in information visualization and offer a basis for developing design guidelines to reduce variability and improve the reliability of LLM-based generative workflows.

title: The Changing Drawing. From Technical Representation to Data Visualization as an Ethical Agent of Society
abstract: This article investigates the contemporary transformation of drawing from a technical instrument of representation into an active device for the interpretation, mediation, and communication of complex information. Within the post-digital condition, where analog and digital dimensions converge into integrated environments of knowledge production, drawing no longer functions merely as a tool for reproducing reality but increasingly operates as a critical and interpretative practice. The study develops an interdisciplinary framework situated at the intersection of visual semiotics, visual studies, digital humanities, and the ethics of images, analysing how diagrams and data visualizations shape the perception and understanding of social, environmental, economic, and political phenomena. Particular attention is devoted to the rhetorical dimension of visualization and to the ethical responsibility embedded in graphic languages. Through references to the theories of Jacques Bertin, Edward Tufte, Alberto Cairo, and Johanna Drucker, the article discusses how visual variables, selection processes, and representational strategies influence both the readability of information and the construction of meaning. Historical and contemporary case studies –from ISOTYPE to recent exhibitions such as Diagrams at Fondazione Prada and Inequalities at the Milan Triennale– demonstrate the central role of graphic sciences in fostering critical awareness and visual literacy. The article argues that contemporary drawing possesses a form of agency: it mediates between informational complexity and human understanding while actively influencing social behaviours and decision-making processes. Consequently, the future of drawing lies in the development of an ʻethics of the sign,’ grounded in transparency, accessibility, and intellectual honesty, capable of contributing to a conscious and democratic visual citizenship.
